newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ credit-tightening unlikely until Oct--analysts.
newsitem.headline: BOJ credit-tightening unlikely until Oct--analysts.

text.p: The Bank of Japan (BOJ) is unlikely to raise interest rates until October at the earliest, despite mounting political pressure for an early credit-tightening, traders and economists said on Monday.
They said uncertainty about Japan's economic outlook and worries about the health of the financial sector are likely to delay any change in monetary policy.
"The BOJ has been saying all along that it wants to examine the scope and strength of the economic recovery," said Yasunari Ueno, chief market economist for Fuji Securities Co Ltd's research group.

"Right now, neither of these is sufficient (for an interest rate rise)," he added. He predicted that the BOJ will raise short-term interest rates possibly as early as October, but said the central bank would not be able to raise the discount rate until late in the current fiscal year.
Ueno said many banks are still saddled with problem loans and that the BOJ will probably be reluctant to raise rates immediately in such an environment.

"It is unclear what will happen to banks'...profits once interest rates are raised... Their fund-raising costs will go up, but it is not clear whether banks will be able to raise the interest charged on their loans in the same manner," he said.
Hidenobu Furuhashi, manager of Toyo Trust & Banking Co Ltd's trading department, also saw October as a plausible time for a rate increase.

He said this would depend, however, on Tokyo share prices holding above the key 20,000 level on the key Nikkei 225 index and the BOJ's "tankan" corporate sentiment survey in July and October showing that the impact of April's sales tax increase was light.

He also said criticism of Japan's ultra-low interest rate policy has intensified recently, and against that backdrop a 50 basis point rise in Japan's official discount rate (ODR) to one percent is likely to be considered reasonable.
The BOJ lowered the ODR to a record-low 0.5 percent on September 8, 1995.

"It has been argued that low interest rates are hurting people who rely on pensions for income... (And) I think it is true that low interest rates have a negative impact on (institutional investors such as) life insurers' investment returns," Furuhashi said.
"A rise in the ODR would not be so much a credit-tightening by the BOJ, but would be more a reflection of their desire to restore interest rates to more normal levels," Furuhashi said.

Noboru Kawai, economic strategist at Morgan Stanley Japan Ltd, was more circumspect, arguing that the BOJ will probably be unable to raise rates until next business year, when the effects of fiscal policy changes such as the consumption tax increase and cuts in public spending become clearer.

"But I think comments suggesting the BOJ is contemplating a rate increase will probably continue to be issued in order to prevent the market from forming a...(concrete) judgment on (the BOJ's) policy decisions," Kawai said.

If the market comes to believe that interest rates will not be raised for some time and takes positions in the market accordingly, it would increase the economic cost of raising interest rates, and the BOJ will want to prevent that, he said.

Speculation about a Japanese rate increase was fuelled last Friday by Eisuke Sakakibara, a senior Finance Ministry official, when he told a French newspaper that a one-half percentage point rise in Japan's discount rate would still leave it at a low level, and that such a move should be expected from the BOJ in the coming year.

Also last week, an executive of a major Japanese labour group told BOJ deputy governor Toshihiko Fukui that while Japan's "super-low interest rate policy" had contributed to economic recovery, it also had adverse effects such as lower interest income on people's savings.

There has also been speculation in Japanese financial markets since the Finance Ministry ordered Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Co to halt operations in late April that the BOJ may raise interest rates to boost institutional investors' investment returns.
